items.item: A table can look fully erased to every normal reader (merge-on-read hides the row) long before the data is actually freed (compaction rewrites it away) — the gap between those two moments is exactly where an over-confident compliance claim goes wrong.

items.item: A replica, a backup and a Kafka topic are not edge cases of the table's own erasure — they are architecturally separate stores that no table-level operation was ever designed to reach, which is why each needs its own closing mechanism.

items.item: Topic 5's crypto-shredding mechanism (introduced there only as a consequence of deleting a key) becomes this topic's main erasure tool precisely because it is indifferent to where a copy of the ciphertext physically sits — the table, the topic, and the backup are all just storage to it.

at.topic: Envelope encryption, KMS and key rotation

items.item: The classification step that tags a column as personal data in the first place is what makes crypto-shredding's own scope question answerable: without knowing which rows belong to a subject, there's no way to say which key should have encrypted them.

Masking a column (topic 8) and erasing a subject's data (this topic) solve different problems: a mask hides a value from an unauthorised reader while the value still exists; erasure is removing the value, or making it permanently unreadable, for everyone.

at.topic: Row/column security and dynamic masking in-engine
at.quote: bypass paths (direct file reads, extracts, unprotected materialized views)

items.item: Writing retention and crypto-shredding decisions as code is the same policy-as-code idea topic 7 applied to who may read a row, applied here to how long a row is allowed to exist at all.

Proof of erasure has two independent parts that must both hold: the table's own metadata (no live snapshot references the subject's files) and the key store's own record (exactly when a key was destroyed) — neither one alone is sufficient, since a table could still be vacuumed while a key survives, or vice versa.

items.item: The predict question's second scenario (a key shredded with no table DELETE ever run) tests whether the reader has separated the two mechanisms entirely: crypto-shredding changes what a stored value decrypts to, never whether a row exists in the table at all.
